newsitem.title: USA: CFTC head sounds warning on U.S. futures law plan.
newsitem.headline: CFTC head sounds warning on U.S. futures law plan.

text.p: The nation's top futures market regulator warned Thursday that a Senate proposal aimed at revising commodity laws would lead to "pervasive deregulation," opening the door for potential fraud and other abuses.

"Our experience in this country continues to demonstrate that there are significant problems associated with futures exchange trading that require vigilant oversight by our agency," Commodity Futures Trading Commission Chairman Brooksley Born said at a news conference here.
Born said her regulatory counterparts overseas were "appalled" when they learned of the U.S. plan.

Born expressed particular concern about a provision of a bill filed by Senate Agriculture Committee leaders that would create "professional markets" that would no longer be subject to a variety of CFTC regulations.
Born noted that foreign regulators have been making changes allowing them to more closely police their own markets in an effort to emulate tough U.S. rules.

"They look to us to set the standards," she said. "In order for us to regulate our markets properly, the CFTC has long believed that it is essential for foreign regulators to regulate their markets well."
Born maintained that the CFTC requires a "panoply" of regulatory tools to watch for fraudulent activity.
She said the agency's ability to enforce anti-fraud rules would be hampered if Congress were to eliminate a range of other futures market regulations.
"You can't merely have an anti-fraud rule because you don't really need affirmatively to make a misrepresentation in order to bilk the public," she said.

Born called futures contracts "speculative instruments" and said regulatory provisions are needed to protect members of the public who may attempt to dabble in the markets without understanding how they work.

"Futures present very different problems from securities and other kinds of investments," she said. "They are not investments. They are speculative instruments -- at least that's how they're being used when they're being sold to the public."
